<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, FlashSpace is a macOS desktop application – a virtual workspace manager designed to replace and enhance native macOS Spaces. It specializes in fast workspace switching, hotkey-based controls, multi-display support, and integrations (e.g., SketchyBar) while keeping a non-intrusive, performance-focused approach. The solution is implemented in Swift, using Xcode (with XcodeGen for project generation) and relying on native macOS APIs and some workarounds for features like Picture-in-Picture mode.

Below are the detailed instructions to design a comprehensive and accurate system design diagram for FlashSpace:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Entry Point & Core App Logic:
     - Components in FlashSpace/App (FlashSpaceApp, AppDelegate, AppDependencies, Migrations) represent the entry point and core life-cycle management.
   • Feature Modules:
     - FlashSpace/Features contains modular components for each feature: FocusManager (window and app focus switching), HotKeys (managing configurable hotkeys), Integrations (interfacing with external applications/systems), MenuBar (display and interaction with the macOS menu bar), PictureInPicture (handling experimental PiP capabilities), Profiles (configuration management), Settings (user preferences and configuration views), SpaceControl (preview and control of workspaces), and Workspaces (defining and managing workspaces).
   • UI Components:
     - FlashSpace/UI holds custom UI elements (Alerts, InputDialog, Toast notifications, HotKeyControl) to deliver user interactions and notifications.
     - FlashSpace/Main deals with the main view and its corresponding view model.
   • Utilities & Extensions:
     - FlashSpace/Utils offers support services such as Autostart, FileChooser, PermissionsManager, and UpdatesManager.
     - FlashSpace/Extensions provides helper extensions for common types and functionality that enable cleaner code throughout the application.
   • Assets & Resources:
     - The Assets.xcassets directory contains all graphical resources (icons and color sets) that support the UI.
   • Project & Build Infrastructure:
     - Files like project.yml, the Xcode project (FlashSpace.xcodeproj), and fastlane configurations indicate the build and deployment setup.
     - GitHub workflows and configuration files support continuous integration and quality checks.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The Core Application interacts with multiple feature modules, invoking specialized managers (like the FocusManager or SpaceControl) based on user input or system events.
   • UI components bind to feature view models (e.g., MainViewModel and SpaceControlViewModel) to reflect live status and control state.
   • The Features interact with each other (e.g., HotKeys may trigger workspace changes managed by the WorkspaceManager; MenuBar features display workspace info) and with Utils for system tasks such as launching, configuration updates, and permission handling.
   • Extensions provide common functionality that is used across features and the core app to simplify tasks like handling shortcuts, manipulating views, or formatting strings.
   • There is also an external service integration part (e.g., SketchyBar integration) which is triggered by changes in the workspace state and handled via configurable scripts.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularization: Each major functionality (workspace management, window focus, hotkey management, settings) is encapsulated in its own module under the Features directory.
   • MVVM for UI: The code includes clear separation between View (MainView, SpaceControlView, etc.) and ViewModel components.
   • Extensions and Utility Layers: The code leverages Swift’s extension mechanism to add common functionalities and maintain DRY code.
   • Clean Separation of Concerns: Core services (e.g., AppDependencies, Migrations) are isolated from UI and feature-specific logic.

4. Tailor the Diagram to the Project Type:
   • Since this is a macOS application with multiple interconnected features, the diagram should clearly separate:
     - Frontend/UI Layer: Illustrate the view components, main window, and UI controls.
     - Business Logic or Feature Layer: Depict the major feature modules (FocusManager, HotKeys, PictureInPicture, etc.) and their interactions.
     - System & Utility Layer: Show shared utilities, extensions, and the integration with external systems (like SketchyBar).
     - Infrastructure: Outline the build processes (XcodeGen, Fastlane, GitHub workflows) and dependencies.

5. Diagram Elements and Visual Guidelines:
   • Use clear labels for each component, for instance “Core App”, “Focus Manager”, “HotKeys”, “Workspace Manager”, “Settings”, “UI Components”, “Utilities/Extensions”, and “External Integration (SketchyBar)”.
   • Represent data flows and interactions using directional arrows. For example, an arrow from “HotKeyManager” to “WorkspaceManager” to indicate that hotkey events trigger workspace switches.
   • Apply distinct shapes or color coding to differentiate between layers:
         – Rectangles for core components and services.
         – Rounded rectangles for UI/view entities.
         – Different colors to segregate UI, business logic/features, and utility/integration modules.
   • Include deployment/build infrastructure components on the side—such as CI/CD pipelines (GitHub workflows, Fastlane) and project generation (XcodeGen) processes—to give a full perspective on the project’s ecosystem.

6. Final Detailed Steps for the Principal Software Engineer:
   a. Start by sketching the top-level structure:
         - Place the Core App at the center.
         - Surround it with the major feature modules (e.g., Focus Manager, HotKeys, SpaceControl, Settings, Workspaces).
         - Indicate the UI components (MainView, MenuBar, etc.) connected to these features.
   b. Draw utility layers and extensions separately, linking them to all modules that use common functionality.
   c. Add in external integrations (such as SketchyBar) to illustrate how the app interfaces with external systems.
   d. Connect the CI/build components (XcodeGen, fastlane, GitHub workflows) outside the runtime architecture, perhaps at the bottom of the diagram, to show development process integration.
   e. Ensure every component is clearly labeled, with directional arrows wherever one component sends events or data to another.
   f. Use annotations to highlight critical design decisions such as the “non-disruptive behavior” and the deliberate avoidance of managing individual app windows per workspace.

Following these guidelines, the resulting diagram will serve as a detailed blueprint that accurately mirrors FlashSpace’s architecture, reflects its modular design and integration points, and is specifically tailored to a macOS virtual workspace manager. This visualization should help stakeholders quickly understand the roles, interactions, and technical stacks that power the application.
</explanation>
